name: practice
description: How the decision-making itself shows up on the page. Check rules are pass or fail; advisory rules are questions the board asks the author and records. No text reused.

rules.title: Each decision states the problem it solves, without naming the solution
rules.requirement: The decision's context describes the situation and the forces at play before the chosen option appears, so a reader could evaluate alternatives from the context alone.

rules.title: Rejected options are listed with the reason each was rejected
rules.requirement: At least one alternative is named for the decision and the text says why it lost. A decision with no alternatives considered fails unless the text says none existed and why.

source.name: Andrew Harmel-Law
source.locator: Facilitating Software Architecture, Chapter 6, Architectural Decision Records

rules.title: The trade-off is explicit, naming what was given up
rules.requirement: The decision names the characteristic it favours and the characteristic it sacrifices, for example consistency over availability, or simplicity over flexibility.

source.name: Neal Ford
source.locator: Software Architecture: The Hard Parts, Chapter 1, Trade-off analysis

rules.title: Reversibility is stated
rules.question: Is this a one-way door or a two-way door? What would it cost to reverse it in a year, and what would it cost to defer it until more is known?

source.name: Gregor Hohpe
source.locator: The Software Architect Elevator, Chapter on selling options

rules.title: The decision traces to a business driver
rules.question: Which business outcome does this decision serve, and how would you explain the choice to the executive who owns that outcome in one sentence?

source.name: Gregor Hohpe
source.locator: The Software Architect Elevator, riding the elevator

rules.title: Who was consulted and who is affected
rules.question: Who gave advice on this decision, which teams are affected by it, and have they seen it in this form?

source.name: Andrew Harmel-Law
source.locator: Facilitating Software Architecture, Chapter 3, The Advice Process

rules.title: Modules are deep, not pass-through
rules.requirement: Where the decision introduces a layer or a component, the text shows it hides meaningful complexity behind a small interface rather than forwarding calls with little added value.

source.name: John Ousterhout
source.locator: A Philosophy of Software Design, Chapter 4, Modules Should Be Deep

rules.title: Goals and non-goals are stated
rules.requirement: The document says what the system must do and explicitly what it will not do or not optimise for, so scope creep is visible.

source.name: George Fairbanks
source.locator: Just Enough Software Architecture, Chapter 3, Risk-Driven Model

rules.title: Quality attributes are ranked, not just listed
rules.requirement: The document names the quality attributes that matter and puts them in priority order, so trade-offs between decisions can be resolved consistently.

source.name: Len Bass
source.locator: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed., Part II, Quality Attributes

rules.title: Stakeholders and their concerns are named
rules.requirement: The document lists who has a stake in the system, such as users, operators, security, finance, and which part of the document addresses each of their concerns.

source.name: Paul Clements and colleagues
source.locator: Documenting Software Architectures, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, Views and Beyond

rules.title: Design depth follows risk
rules.requirement: The riskiest parts of the system get the most design attention, and the document says which parts it deliberately leaves shallow and why.

source.name: George Fairbanks
source.locator: Just Enough Software Architecture, Chapter 3, Risk-Driven Model

rules.title: The service tier is stated
rules.requirement: The document says how critical the service is, for example a tier or classification, so that the expected level of reliability, monitoring and security can be read from it.

rules.title: Open questions and known risks are listed
rules.requirement: The document has a section listing what is undecided, what is uncertain and what could invalidate the design, each with an owner or a date.

source.name: Michael Keeling
source.locator: Design It!, Chapter 5, Dig for Architecturally Significant Requirements

rules.title: Can the design be explained at two altitudes
rules.question: Give the two-sentence version of this design for an executive, and the two-sentence version for the engineer who will be on call for it. Do both versions say the same thing?

rules.title: Architectural thinking is visible, not just technology choice
rules.question: Which decision in this document would you make differently if the team were twice the size, or half? What does that tell you about which constraints are really driving the design?
